metric.why: Annual matching and hourly matching are very different claims; hourly carbon-free matching is the harder standard the largest operators now report progress against. Reading which claim is being made matters more than the percentage.
metric.definition: The share of facility consumption matched by renewable generation, reported either as annual matching through purchased certificates or as around-the-clock hourly matching.

reading.body:
How a data center reports renewable energy use matters more than the percentage itself; annual matching through certificates and hourly matching are fundamentally different claims about carbon footprint.

Annual matching allows a facility to purchase renewable credits covering its yearly consumption without requiring that power actually flow to the building when it operates. Hourly matching requires renewable generation to feed the grid simultaneously with facility demand, a much stricter constraint. The largest data center operators have begun reporting hourly matching because it represents genuine grid decarbonization rather than accounting reconciliation. Which standard an operator cites reveals whether their sustainability claim tracks physical power flows or spreadsheet offsets.

For AI infrastructure, this distinction shapes how much renewable energy actually reaches compute clusters as they scale. A facility reporting annual matching at 95% may still draw coal power during peak demand hours when renewables are unavailable. Hourly matching exposes the real challenge: aligning massive compute workloads with solar and wind generation patterns. This constraint grows tighter as data center power consumption rises, making the grid's renewable capacity and storage capabilities the actual bottleneck, not the renewable energy that exists somewhere in the system.

This metric does not quantify total facility efficiency, water usage, or embodied carbon in hardware and construction. It also does not track whether reported renewable generation is new capacity or existing infrastructure rebranded, a distinction that matters for whether data centers drive grid decarbonization or merely claim it.
